faq_slots.question: Why does water sit on my drive after rain?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Use the assigned symptom's meaning and its linked local issue. Three genuinely different causes in plain words: a fall never built into the base, so the rain has nowhere to run; ground underneath that has softened and let the surface sink into a dip; nowhere for the water to go, because there is no drain or soakaway, or a surface that was meant to let the rain through has joints full of silt. Then what the local ground adds, then the fix, which starts with finding out whether the base is still sound.

faq_slots.question: Which driveway surface suits a front garden?
faq_slots.answer_brief: What decides it, in order: whether the rain can pass through the surface or run to a border or soakaway inside the garden (a surface that does usually keeps a front garden outside a planning application; one that sends the rain to the road usually does not; no area figure), the slope, how the drive is used and what is under it now, and how it looks against the house last. Say which surfaces let the rain through from the trade facts (gravel, permeable block paving, resin bound over a base that drains) and name an option for this business only from [CV: materials_methods]. No claim about how long one lasts against another: the facts give none.

faq_slots.question: Can a driveway be laid in winter?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Yes in principle, with the reasons the day is chosen, from the trade facts timing cells: a base cannot be compacted on frozen or saturated ground; tarmac has to be rolled before it cools, so a cold windy day is avoided; fresh concrete is protected from frost and from drying too fast while it cures; resin is laid inside its system's weather limits and kept dry while it cures. So the work runs through most of the year with days moved by the weather. No dates, no promise about the weather, nothing about this business's own timings.

faq_slots.question: Do I need planning permission for a new driveway?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Point at the trade facts rule rows (Table C) and write what usually applies, with "usually" or "in most cases": a new surface at the front of the house usually stays outside a planning application when the rain can pass through it or runs onto a border, a lawn or a soakaway inside the garden, and usually needs one when it sends the rain to the road; a patio at the back usually needs none; the council whose road it is usually has to agree before the kerb is lowered, and a classified main road adds a planning application. What the customer does about it only as the row gives it; whether this business handles the application only from [CV: handles_planning]. No figure, no area, never an Act's or an order's name. Conservation areas and listed homes can add controls: say so without naming them.

cards.title: Nowhere to park off the street
cards.brief: A situation card, not a fault: the car lives on the road, the front garden is a lawn nobody uses or a shared drive too narrow for two cars. What decides it: the depth of the frontage (whether a car fits without hanging over the pavement), the kerb (a full height kerb means the council whose road it is usually has to agree to a crossing before anything else), and where the rain will go (a surface the rain can pass through, or a fall to a border or soakaway inside the garden, usually keeps a front garden outside a planning application; a solid surface that sends the rain to the road usually does not; no area figure, never the rule's name). Never kerb appeal, never a promise about the council's answer, never a fault invented for it.
cards.mechanism: a frontage with no drive to park on

cards.title: Ruts, dips and blocks that rock
cards.brief: Problem led: tyre tracks that have dipped, a block that rocks underfoot, blocks spreading at the edge, sand gone from the gaps with weeds rooted in the dirt that replaced it, a slab that has sunk. The one cause this card makes: what is under the surface was never built for the weight of a car (a base too thin or never compacted, soft ground left in, edging that gave so the blocks spread, joints emptied of sand so the blocks lose their grip on each other). Say what the fix involves in plain words from the trade facts stages: the failed area lifted, what supports it repaired, then the surface relaid; and the diagnosis the repair customer wants: blocks that have sunk over a base that is still sound can be lifted and relaid, a base that has failed across the drive cannot be patched for long. Weeds root in the joints from above, in the dirt that collects there, so a membrane underneath is not the answer (Table E). By category: Concrete Contractor reads it as a slab that rocks or has sunk, with cracks widening; Road Construction Company as wheel ruts and edges breaking under turning traffic. No depth or figure the rows do not give; never a dig at another trade.
cards.mechanism: a base too thin or too soft for the weight on it

cards.title: Puddles that stay after the rain has gone
cards.brief: Problem led: water by the front door or the garage, a puddle in the tyre tracks, a drive that was meant to let the rain through now holding it because the joints are full of silt. The one cause this card makes: the fall was never built in, or there is nowhere for the water to go. Say what the fix usually involves from the trade facts stages: the falls set in the base before the surface goes down (never made up in the sand bed, Table E), a channel drain across a drive that falls towards the house, a soakaway or a border inside the garden to take it, an open stone base kept clean of fines under a permeable surface. Say what water left standing does: it works into the base below and softens it, and beside the house it sits against the wall. What the business does on site only from confirmed practices. Never promise the ground will change. By category: Concrete Contractor reads it as water pooling on a slab laid to the wrong falls; Road Construction Company as standing water across the bays. Not slow draining ground on its own: the symptom FAQ may own that.
cards.mechanism: a fall never built in, and nowhere for the water to go

cards.title: A back garden you cross on wet grass
cards.brief: A situation card: the back door opens onto grass or onto an old patio of cracked slabs, the bins and the shed are reached across the lawn, a step down from the door lands on nothing. What decides it: the levels at the door and the fall away from the house, the ground there, and how the household uses the garden. What the work gives them, in plain words: a patio laid to fall away from the house, a path that is a path in every weather, steps with treads that do not rock. By category: Paving reads it as the patio, path or steps and their base; Concrete Contractor as a concrete base or path, or an imprinted patio and the sealer it will need looking after (schedule led: what slips and when, the reason in the sealer worn by feet and sun, never the diary); Road Construction Company as a footway or forecourt laid to a fall, only where the services list carries a car park page. Never a lifestyle pitch, never a fault invented for it.
cards.mechanism: no level, dry surface where the garden is used

cards.brief: The things a homeowner notices first, from the trade facts signs row, in their words: the same dip back again, a patch broken at its edge, chippings coming loose, the old coat peeling or gone white, paving green and slippery, bay lines faded. The one cause this card makes: the job left undone. Then what it leads to if left, from the skipped column: water gets into the break and weakens what is under it, and every car that passes makes the opening bigger; specific, never alarming. On a schedule led page (driveway sealing, resealing imprinted concrete, driveway and patio cleaning, car park line marking) the card is what slips and when, with the reason in the material and never in the customer's diary: a sealer thinned by tyres and sun so the colour fades and oil marks stay in; joints clogged with dirt that weeds root into from above; lines worn faint where the traffic turns. cards.title: The same dip keeps coming back
cards.brief: A repair that has sunk again, blocks rocking round a patch, a crack reopening through a concrete repair, a pothole back through the dressing. The one cause this card makes: the surface was replaced without the support under it being put right. Say what the job does underneath so it stays put, from the trade facts stages and the done badly row: the drainage looked at first, the failed material lifted or cut out, what supports it repaired, then the surface reinstated and compacted; an overlay does not correct a base that moves, and a dressing over a pothole shows it again. No depth or figure the rows do not give; never a dig at another trade. On a schedule led page: what a season's wear has moved, from the signs row (joints that have lost their sand so blocks shift; a patch of sealer worn through where the car turns).

cards.title: Getting what's underneath right first
cards.brief: The customer's situation: they have had a cheap quote, or a knock at the door from someone with tarmac left over from a job nearby, and want to know what the difference buys. What decides it: the layers they will never see once it is finished (the dig to firm ground, the base compacted in layers with the falls made in it, the edging bedded and backed in concrete, the drainage), which is where a quick job cuts corners and where it gives way inside a couple of winters. What the work gives them: those layers done as the trade facts stages name them for this service, so the surface stays where it was laid; on resin bound and tar and chip, the old surface underneath checked and made sound first, because a thin new layer shows up whatever is wrong underneath; on concrete, the joints formed and the slab protected while it cures; on a dropped kerb, a crossing built to the council's own specification and inspected by it. One specific from the stages for this service; no depth or figure the rows do not give; never a dig at another trade. A written quote before any work starts only when the written_quote practice is confirmed.
cards.mechanism: the layers underneath, which decide how long it stays put

cards.title: Which surface suits your frontage
cards.brief: The customer's situation: they are weighing two or three ways of doing it (blocks against resin against gravel against tarmac against concrete; porcelain against natural stone against concrete flags on a patio; a fixed, removable or retractable bollard). What decides it: whether the rain has to pass through the surface or can run to a border inside the garden, the slope (loose gravel on a slope wants a grid to hold it), how the drive is used (turning, a van, a trailer), what is under it now (resin bound and tar and chip want a sound base beneath; a failed one comes out first), how much looking after they want, and how it looks against the house last, from the trade facts materials and methods cell for this service. What the work gives them: the option that suits their frontage, never the one that is best in general. A named product only from [CV: materials_methods]. No claim about how long one lasts against another, and no price comparison, unless the rows or the client values give it (Table G: none found). On the Dropped kerbs page there is no option to weigh: the council's specification decides, so the card is what the council will and will not agree to.
cards.mechanism: the rain, the slope and the use deciding the surface

cards.title: What it needs from you afterwards
cards.brief: The customer's situation: they want to know what they are taking on once the job is done. What decides it: what the new surface needs to settle and then through the year, from the trade facts stages, timing cell and Table E for this service: time kept off it before a car goes on, which depends on the material and the weather and is given only as the facts' cell gives it; joint sand brushed back in when it is lost; a permeable drive's joints kept clear of soil and leaves so the water can still get through; gravel raked back and topped up; imprinted concrete resealed as its sealer wears, an interval only as the facts' product advice gives it and never promised; ordinary block paving needing no sealer at all. What the work gives them: an honest picture of what it saves them and what it does not. Never a promise about how it will look or last; a cleaning or sealing visit offered only where the services list has one.
cards.mechanism: what the new surface needs to settle in and stay draining

cards.title: Ground that moves under a drive
cards.brief: Drives that have dipped in the tyre tracks, slabs that have tilted, cracks across concrete, water that stands for days. The one cause this card makes: the ground under the town's streets; the town profile and a symptom say which ground (clay that holds water and shrinks and swells with the seasons, chalk or sand that drains freely, a river valley, made ground on a new estate). Say what it means for any job that goes into the ground, in plain words: the dig, the base the ground needs, where the water can be sent; never a depth or a figure, never a promise the ground will change. Not a base too thin for the weight, not a fall never built in: the town's category and service pages own those.
cards.mechanism: the ground under the town's streets

cards.title: Frontages laid out before the car
cards.brief: A front too shallow for a car to sit on without hanging over the pavement, a shared drive between semis, a verge between the garden and the road. The one cause this card makes: front gardens laid out for a street with no cars on it, which the town profile dates (terraces near the centre with shallow fronts, interwar semis with room for a car in front, post war estates with shared drives and verges). Tie the era to what the work involves and never to a judgement on today's frontages: on a shallow front the question is a surface that drains and a path, not a parking space; on a deeper one a drive sized to the house's cars; on a shared drive, whose land the edge sits on. What the business does only from confirmed practices.
cards.mechanism: front gardens laid out for a street with no cars on it

cards.title: Kerbs the council has to agree to
cards.brief: A full height kerb outside a house with room to park, a crossing that was never agreed, a tree or a lamp post where the kerb would need to drop. The one cause this card makes: the pavement belongs to the council whose road it is, so the council has to agree before it is lowered, and a classified main road adds a planning application ("usually", never the Act's name). What the town adds, from the profile and the research only: the classified roads through the town, trees on the pavement line and lamp posts that fix where a kerb can drop, controlled parking zones where the research confirms them. Never the council's process, fees or timescales unless the research gives them, never its approved contractors, never a promise about its answer.
cards.mechanism: a crossing the council has to agree to

cards.title: Rain with nowhere to go on a paved street
cards.brief: A street where every front has been paved and the rain runs off them all onto the road, a gully that cannot keep up in a downpour, a front that falls towards the house. The one cause this card makes: rain running off paved fronts with nowhere to soak in; the town profile and the research say where (surface water flood risk where it is confirmed, a slope towards the houses, a low street). Say what usually applies to a new front surface (the rain passing through it, or a fall to a border or a soakaway inside the garden) and what a front that falls towards the house usually needs (a channel drain across it), in plain words and never the rule's name. Not water on one drive or one patio: the service pages own that.
cards.mechanism: rain running off paved fronts with nowhere to soak in

cost.h2: What Affects the Cost of [WORK] in [TOWN]

cards.title: Getting a digger onto the frontage
cards.brief: On a terraced street the digger, the skip and the waste lorry all work from the road, with parking to clear and a skip that has to sit on the highway. Say why that adds time (never "the only way": a superlative); the town profile says which streets are terraced. No figure.

cards.title: Frontages that fall towards the house
cards.brief: A front garden that slopes down to the door needs its falls designed, a channel drain across it and more digging at the top than a flat one. Say it plainly, from the town profile where it gives the slope. No figure.

cards.title: Conservation areas and classified roads
cards.brief: Where the town has conservation areas with front garden controls, or the house sits on a classified road, the application before the work can start adds time, and some things cannot be done at all. "Usually", never the order's or the area's official name. From the dossier rules only; otherwise the council's consent for a crossing as something that usually applies.

cards.title: What is under the old drive
cards.brief: Tarmac laid over old concrete, a doorstep trader's overlay over a base that had already failed, made ground on a new estate, an old path under the lawn: what has to come out and be taken away before anything new goes in. What the town's housing era usually left in the ground, from the profile only, said as what the work meets and never as a judgement on the drives. How it is taken away only from confirmed practices. No figure.

faq_slots.answer_brief: From [CV: quote_method] and the confirmed practices only: what the customer sends, what the business looks at, what comes back. Where the town's roads or front garden controls bring a rule in, say it is settled before the design, with "usually"; whether the business handles the application only from [CV: handles_planning]. No timescale unless [CV: response_time] is set.

faq_slots.question: When is the best time of year for [WORK_LOWER] work?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Most of the year, with the reasons a laying day is chosen from the trade facts timing cells: a base cannot be compacted on frozen or saturated ground; tarmac has to be rolled before it cools; fresh concrete is kept from frost while it cures; resin goes down dry, inside its system's limits. Where the town profile gives the ground (clay still wet in spring, chalk dry early), say what it does to that window. Nothing about spring being busy or booking ahead. No dates, no promises about the weather, never this business's own laying or curing times.
